question: Verify and extend a Phase 1 analysis of Razorpay's real business problems as of Aug 2026: falsify eight established findings (UPI AutoPay mandate revocations and SBI auto-debit approval rates, blended UPI success vs technical decline split, T+2 settlement vs RBI PA Directions 2025 T+1 mandate, merchant fund holds with no covering agent, refunds as top complaint category, Vulcan's unaudited performance claims, confidentially pre-filed DRHP, Agent Studio's seven beta agents), and fill missing magnitudes (COD RTO rate and cost, refund failure rate, Indian SME DSO and MSME delayed payments, cart abandonment and Magic Checkout effect, merchant-side fraud/chargeback rates, reconciliation FTE effort, subscription involuntary churn) — prioritising Razorpay engineering blog, Razorpay research reports, 2026 leadership interviews, RazorpayX pages, developer docs, and 2026 newsroom.
summary: The question mixes two research modes: refutation of specific dated claims, which needs primary sources (NPCI statistics, RBI directions, SEBI filings, Razorpay's own docs), and quantification of unmeasured problems, which needs industry benchmarks and practitioner data. Each angle therefore targets a different source family and a disjoint cluster of claims, with one dedicated merchant-complaint/contrarian angle and one dedicated Razorpay-primary-source angle so the falsification set and the magnitude set do not overlap.

angles.label: Regulator primary data (falsifies claims 1-2)
angles.query: NPCI UPI AutoPay e-mandate statistics 2026 monthly mandate revocation insufficient balance auto-debit approval rate bank-wise SBI decline technical decline percentage
angles.rationale: Claims 1 and 2 rest on NPCI's monthly AutoPay and UPI decline datasets; only NPCI/RBI primary statistics can show whether the Sep-2025 figures still hold in 2026 and how technical vs business decline now splits.

angles.label: Regulation vs practice: settlement and fund holds (claims 3-4)
angles.query: RBI Payment Aggregator Directions 2025 settlement T+1 timeline compliance versus Razorpay settlement cycle T+2 merchant fund hold account freeze reserve balance policy
angles.rationale: Tests the regulation-vs-practice gap against the RBI master direction text and Razorpay's published settlement and reserve-balance documentation, and surfaces fund-hold triggers and resolution bands from official rather than marketing sources.

angles.label: Merchant complaints and contrarian evidence (claims 4-5, refund failure rate)
angles.query: Razorpay merchant complaints 2026 refund failed delayed settlement withheld reviews Trustpilot MouthShut consumer complaint forum RBI ombudsman digital transactions annual report refund complaint share
angles.rationale: Refunds-as-top-complaint and fund-holds-as-live-problem must be tested against independent merchant-review and ombudsman complaint data, which also yields an actual refund failure/delay percentage instead of a plausible guess.

angles.label: Razorpay primary sources: engineering, docs, newsroom, leadership (claims 6-8)
angles.query: engineering.razorpay.com blog 2026 architecture postmortem scale Razorpay Agent Studio early access agents Harshil Mathur Shashank Kumar interview 2026 AI agents Vulcan methodology DRHP SEBI confidential pre-filing status
angles.rationale: Covers the un-reached source types (engineering blog, developer docs, leadership interviews, newsroom) and claims 6-8 in one pass: engineering posts and docs expose unsolved problems and 'contact support' escape hatches, while 2026 interviews and filings settle DRHP status, Agent Studio scope, and any Vulcan baseline.

angles.label: E-commerce and risk magnitudes: RTO, abandonment, chargebacks
angles.query: India cash on delivery return to origin RTO rate percentage ecommerce 2026 cost per RTO shipment Indian ecommerce cart abandonment rate benchmark Magic Checkout conversion uplift merchant chargeback fraud rate India report
angles.rationale: Fills the e-commerce and risk half of the magnitude gap using logistics and consultancy benchmarks (Shiprocket, Unicommerce, Redseer, Baymard India), which is where RTO, abandonment and merchant-side chargeback rates actually live, given RBI bank-fraud data is explicitly invalid as a proxy.

angles.label: B2B receivables, DSO and finance-ops effort magnitudes
angles.query: MSME Samadhaan delayed payment claims amount 2026 India SME average days sales outstanding DSO TReDS trade receivables discounting volume finance team hours spent on payment reconciliation India survey
angles.rationale: Isolates the finance and revenue magnitude gaps (DSO, MSME delayed-payment stock, reconciliation hours/FTEs) which come from government portals, RBI/TReDS data and CFO surveys, sources entirely disjoint from the payments-domain queries above.

results.title: India D2C Report 2026: Operations, RTO & Growth Data — Unicommerce
results.snippet: Highest-value find for JOB 2's RTO magnitude gap: an independent industry-report (not Razorpay marketing) built on 410M+ shipments across 6,000+ Indian D2C brands, FY2026. Hard numbers: RTO 39.2% at festive peak (Nov 2025), 25.6% (Jan 2026), 21.0% (Mar 2026) for brands applying prepaid-incentive + pin-code-routing fixes; COD return rate 58% in the festive quarter vs under 15% prepaid; Tier 2/3 drove 66% of incremental order volume. This gives dated, sourced RTO magnitude for the 'RTO Shield / RTO Insights' agents that Razorpay ships without publishing any benchmark, and supplies the COD-vs-prepaid delta that makes the problem concrete.

results.title: What Is Return To Origin (RTO) In eCommerce? — GoKwik
results.snippet: Supplies the cost-per-RTO figure missing from Phase 1. GoKwik (a direct Razorpay Magic Checkout competitor, so treat as vendor-adjacent but with proprietary transaction data): industry average RTO ~20-25%, up to ~40% by category/pincode; COD RTO ~26% vs under 2% for prepaid; unit economics of ~Rs 285 loss per RTO order on a Rs 1,000 order (Rs 200 forward + Rs 85 reverse). Cross-corroborates Unicommerce's COD/prepaid split from an independent dataset. Note the claimed '30-40% RTO reduction' is GoKwik marketing and must be labelled as such under the CRITICAL RULE.

results.title: What is Cart Abandonment Rate? Exact Formula and Benchmarks — Razorpay Learn
results.snippet: Razorpay-official (Razorpay Learn, dated 29 Jan 2025) source type (b) — Razorpay's own published data content. Quantifies checkout abandonment: global average 70.22% (cited to Baymard), mobile 80.02% vs desktop 66.41%, category bands 57-83%. Critically for the India gap, Razorpay itself states Indian D2C brands convert at ~2% vs Amazon/Flipkart ~10% and attributes the gap to checkout experience. Notably it provides NO Magic Checkout conversion number of its own — only third-party Baymard's 35.26% usability uplift — which is direct evidence that Razorpay publishes no audited baseline for its own checkout product (supports falsification target #6's pattern).

results.title: 50 Cart Abandonment Rate Statistics 2026 — Baymard Institute
results.snippet: The primary source behind the Razorpay Learn numbers, so it lets you verify Razorpay's citation rather than trusting the reseller. Baymard is the standing independent benchmark (aggregated from dozens of studies) for the 70%+ abandonment rate and the reasons-for-abandonment breakdown. Use for the abandonment magnitude cell; the caveat to flag is that Baymard's panel is not India-specific, so the India-specific abandonment number remains an honest partial gap even after this source.

results.title: India digital fraud is twice global average; telecom fraud surged 308% — Business Standard (TransUnion report, June 2026)
results.snippet: Press coverage of TransUnion's 2026 State of Omnichannel Fraud report — a valid alternative to RBI's disallowed >=Rs 1 lakh bank-fraud dataset because it measures transaction-level suspected fraud, not advances. India suspected digital fraud rate 7.1% in 2025 vs 3.8% global; within India, account logins 3.9%, account creation 3.1%, and financial transactions 1.2%. The 1.2% financial-transaction figure is the usable merchant-side fraud magnitude. Dated June 2026, so current. Caveat: 'suspected' fraud is a model flag, not confirmed loss, so it overstates realised chargeback loss and understates nothing — label accordingly.

results.title: Average Chargeback Rate: Benchmarks and Network Thresholds — Chargeback.io
results.snippet: Fills the chargeback-rate magnitude cell and calibrates Razorpay's own stated fund-hold trigger of 'chargeback >1%' (falsification target #4). Reports average all-industry chargeback rate 0.26% of transactions in Q3 2025, up from 0.21% YoY, plus card-network monitoring thresholds (Visa/Mastercard programs) and merchant dispute win rates of 20-30% typical. Shows Razorpay's 1% freeze trigger sits roughly 4x above the industry average rate — i.e. a merchant must be a severe outlier to trip it. Vendor blog (chargeback-services provider), global not India-specific: label industry-report with a vendor caveat.

results.title: 1.8K Razorpay Reviews — PissedConsumer complaint-category breakdown
results.snippet: CONTRARIAN EVIDENCE AGAINST CLAIM 5. Independent complaint-aggregator category split: Payments and Charges 37%, Customer Inquiries & Issues 19%, Account 13%, REFUND 13%, Request for Information 7%, Product/Service 4%, Activation/Cancellation 3%, Shipping/Delivery 1%, Return/Replace 1%. Refunds are therefore NOT the single most frequent complaint category — they tie for third at 13%, well behind 'Payments and Charges' at 37%. Also gives magnitude: 1.7/5 stars across 397 rated reviews (1.8K total), 33% would recommend, 25% issue-resolution rate, customer-service rating 1/5. Source type: merchant/consumer-review aggregator. Caveat: self-selected complainant sample, category taxonomy is the site's own, and 'Payments and Charges' likely absorbs settlement-hold complaints. Use as the numeric basis for a refund-complaint share (13%) rather than the unsupported 'most frequent' claim.

results.title: What to Do When Your Payment Gateway Account Is Frozen: A 2026 Action Plan (Razorpay blog, 9 Jun 2026)
results.snippet: CONFIRMS AND DATES CLAIM 4, with new magnitudes. Razorpay-official content, published 9 June 2026. Six named freeze triggers: chargeback ratio 'consistently cross 1%' (vs global e-commerce average 0.60%; recommended internal alert threshold 0.5%), 10x volume spikes during festive sale/product launch, KYC/PAN/GST/address/director documentation gaps flagged under Payment Aggregator compliance, fraud signals (velocity anomalies, IP mismatch, refund abuse), ToS/MCC violations, and regulatory/legal holds (cybercrime complaints, court orders). Resolution bands confirmed: KYC 2-5 business days, chargeback/fraud review 1-3 weeks, legal/regulatory 30+ days. NEW MAGNITUDE for the fund-hold problem: '44% of merchants reported significant cash-flow stress from unexpected payment holds'; claims centralised data 'can cut compliance handling time by 25 to 30%' — that last figure is Razorpay marketing with no published methodology and must be labelled as such.

results.title: Razorpay Reviews — Trustpilot
results.snippet: Independent merchant-review corroboration of the fund-hold problem and its severity, not just its existence: merchants report accounts 'permanently disabled' citing vague 'violation of Terms of Service' with no clause or evidence cited, funds held 120 days, and settlement blocks where the promised 120-day credit had still not arrived six months later. Establishes that the tail of the freeze distribution is far longer than Razorpay's own '30+ days' band, and that no self-serve product resolves it — merchants escalate via support/social. Source type: merchant-review. Caveat: unverified individual posts; use as existence-and-tail evidence, not as a rate.

results.title: RBI Annual Report of the Ombudsman Scheme 2024-25 — complaint category shares
results.snippet: REGULATOR BASELINE that also weighs against claim 5 at ecosystem level. FY25 total complaints 13,34,244, up 13.55% from 11,75,075 in FY24. Category shares: loans and advances 29.25%, credit cards 17.15%, mobile/electronic banking 16.86%, deposit accounts 16.84%; ATM/debit-card complaints fell from 14.56% (FY23) to 7.47% (FY25). Banks account for 81.53% of complaints. Notably there is NO standalone 'refund not credited' category reported at the top level — so the RB-IOS data does not support 'refunds are the most frequent complaint category', and the aggregator/PA layer is not separately broken out. Honest empty cell: RBI Ombudsman does not publish a Razorpay- or PA-specific complaint count. Fetch the full RBI PDF for the sub-category table if a refund-specific share is required.

results.title: Razorpay consumer complaints and resolution rates — Voxya
results.snippet: Second independent complaint platform giving a resolution-rate magnitude across three Razorpay entities: Razorpay 51.52% satisfaction (17 of 33 complaints resolved), Razorpay Payment Gateway 61.54% (8 of 13), Razorpay Software Private Limited 46.15% (6 of 13). Small-N (total ~59 complaints) so treat as directional only, but it independently corroborates PissedConsumer's low resolution rate (25%) and shows roughly half of escalated merchant/consumer complaints go unresolved — evidence for an OPEN support/dispute-resolution gap. Complaint bodies are dominated by refund-not-received and money-deducted-not-settled narratives.

results.title: Razorpay Review 2026: Fees, Safety & Value for Businesses
results.snippet: Third-party 2026 review that synthesises the merchant-sentiment split and names the dominant negative theme explicitly: sudden account limitations and fund withholding during compliance reviews, triggered by atypical volume spikes or documentation gaps, is what 'dominates negative reviews on Trustpilot and Reddit'. Characterises Razorpay as highly rated by developers but a source of deep frustration once an account is flagged — 'core tech wins praise while support and freezes drive frustration'. Useful for the who_suffers and remaining_gap fields on the fund-hold record. Source type: competitor-adjacent press (xFlow is a payments company), so discount for commercial bias; corroborated independently by Trustpilot and PissedConsumer above.

results.title: Recordent Indian SME Receivables Report 2026: average overdue receivables cross Rs 3.83 crore
results.snippet: Industry-report, released World MSME Day (27 June) 2026. Directly fills the DSO magnitude hole: Indian SMEs take an average of 73 days to settle invoices, and the average SME carries ~Rs 3.83 crore of receivables unpaid for MORE than 360 days. Crucially it kills the 'bad credit policy' explanation: 82.6% of invoices are issued on 0-30 day terms, so the 73-day figure is pure collection failure, not generous terms. Sample: ~1.1 lakh MSMEs, 10+ lakh transaction-level data points — a real dataset, not a vendor claim, though Recordent sells receivables/collections software so treat the framing as interested. This is the single strongest number available for a B2B-receivables/collections agent thesis; note Razorpay has NO product covering it (RazorpayX handles vendor PAYOUTS, i.e. money going out, not receivables coming in).

results.title: MSME SAMADHAAN — Delayed Payment Monitoring System (Ministry of MSME, Govt of India)
results.snippet: Regulator/government primary source and the live counter for delayed-payment stock. As reported from portal data on 14 Aug 2026: 2,56,892 delayed-payment applications filed by micro and small enterprises involving Rs 55,244 crore, of which Rs 20,979 crore remains pending. Breakdown: 52,744 applications (Rs 8,397.25 crore) not yet examined by Facilitation Councils; 47,088 (~Rs 14,243 crore) converted into cases; 53,911 cases (Rs 14,638.38 crore) disposed. ~40,580 applications (16%) unresolved for over a year. This is the government-authored magnitude for MSME delayed payments the Phase 1 analysis was missing — and the 16%/>1-year figure is itself evidence that the statutory remedy is slow, which is the wedge for a software collections/receivables agent. Caveat for the falsification job: Samadhaan only captures disputes ESCALATED to MSEFC, so it is a floor, not the total stock of overdue B2B receivables.

results.title: MSME Bill could be an 'IBC moment' for delayed payments if implemented well: Crisil Intelligence (17 Aug 2026)
results.snippet: Press + rating-agency analysis dated 17 Aug 2026 — within days of the Aug 2026 cutoff, so it is the freshest regulatory-direction evidence. Covers the MSME Development (Amendment) Bill 2026 reforms to delayed payments and MSEFCs and carries the Samadhaan figures (Rs 55,244 crore filed / Rs 20,979 crore pending). Relevance to the Razorpay question: it establishes that B2B delayed payment is a live, legislatively-acknowledged problem in Aug 2026 (not a historical one), and Crisil's 'if implemented well' hedge is direct evidence the enforcement channel remains slow — supporting an OPEN verdict for the RECEIVABLES/collections domain with 'none found' as the current Razorpay solution.

results.title: Adyen — Everything you need to know about financial reconciliation (FTE and workday-loss benchmarks)
results.snippet: Payments-competitor knowledge hub carrying survey figures for the reconciliation-effort hole: 36% of companies lose at least one full workday per week to reconciliation, and many run more than four FTEs on financial reconciliation. Useful as the only quantified reconciliation-effort benchmark surfaced, and it is notable that a payment ACQUIRER publishes it — i.e. a peer of Razorpay treats settlement/recon effort as a named merchant pain. Two caveats that must be labelled: (1) it is a competitor's content-marketing page, so classify as Razorpay-adjacent vendor marketing, not independent research; (2) the sample is global/EU-weighted with NO India-specific split. Flag honestly: no India-specific reconciliation hours/FTE survey was found in this pass.

results.title: RBI Master Direction on Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS), effective 23 June 2026
results.snippet: Regulator source, effective 23 June 2026 — RBI consolidated a decade of TReDS instructions into a single Master Direction. Relevant because TReDS is the state's answer to the same receivables problem Razorpay does not address, and its throughput sizes the addressable gap: ~Rs 1.9 lakh crore of invoices discounted cumulatively through FY2025 (Rs 1.38 lakh crore cumulative vs Rs 76,645 crore at FY2022-23), with 80,000+ MSMEs registered. Read against the Rs 55,244 crore of ESCALATED disputes and Rs 3.83 crore average per-SME overdue stock, TReDS reaches only a fraction of MSMEs — evidence the receivables-financing rail exists but coverage is thin, leaving pre-financing collection/chasing entirely manual. Independent verification of the volume figures against RBI/SIDBI primary data is still needed; the crore figures here came via secondary summaries.

results.title: Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) by industry — 2025 benchmarks and analysis
results.snippet: Provides the global comparator that makes the India number meaningful: Allianz Trade's Global DSO & Working Capital Report 2026 puts world DSO at 56.5 days for 2025 (up 0.3 days YoY), against Recordent's 73-day Indian SME figure — i.e. Indian SMEs wait roughly 16 days longer than the global average, a quantified India-specific penalty. Ranked low because it is a credit-software vendor's aggregation blog rather than the Allianz primary report, and it is industry-benchmark, not India-specific; the Allianz Trade original should be fetched directly before this 56.5-day figure is cited as evidence. Use only as context framing for the Recordent number, never as a standalone source.

results.title: NPCI Plans Unified Dashboard for UPI AutoPay Across All Payment Apps (The420.in, 23 June 2026)
results.snippet: FALSIFICATION ATTEMPT ON CLAIM 1 FAILS — claim is CORROBORATED and refreshed to mid-2026. Verbatim: 'only about 30% of auto-debit transactions are successfully approved' at SBI, 'The remaining 70% fail, predominantly due to business-related issues such as insufficient funds.' Also gives fresh volume magnitude: top-10 remitter banks processed ~1.6 billion e-mandate transactions in May 2026, 'an almost threefold increase compared to the 577 million transactions processed during the same period just one year prior.' This is the single most important result: the Sep-2025 SBI ~30% figure still holds nine months later. CAVEAT for the parent analysis: this is press reporting OF NPCI data, not NPCI primary output — NPCI's own AutoPay statistics page returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the SBI number cannot currently be independently verified against the regulator's own dataset. Source type: press (secondary on regulator data).

results.title: Declined (BD/TD) & Uptime — NPCI official statistics
results.snippet: THE primary regulator dataset for Claim 2. NPCI publishes per-bank monthly Technical Decline (TD, bank/NPCI-side failure) and Business Decline (BD, user-side: wrong PIN, insufficient balance) plus uptime. NPCI Circular OC-149 (June 2022) sets the binding targets: TD <1%, BD <5% — note NPCI's own thresholds concede BD is allowed to be 5x TD, which is structural support for Claim 2's 'residual failure is mostly BUSINESS decline' thesis rather than a refutation. ACCESS FINDING (report as a limitation, not a result): npci.org.in returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to automated fetch on both /statistics/bd-td-and-uptime and /product/ecosystem-statistics/autopay, so no 2026 month-stamped TD/BD figure was obtained from the primary source in this pass — a human browser session or the dataful.in/indiadataportal mirrors are needed. Source type: regulator (primary, unretrieved).

results.title: UPI Payment Success Rates: 2026 Benchmarks and How to Improve Yours (productgrowth.in)
results.snippet: Directly restates Claim 2 and supplies its provenance — which weakens it. Confirms merchant blended success 92-96% ('below 90% indicates a serious business problem'), system-wide TD ~0.7-0.8% in 2025 down from 8-10% in 2016, and NPCI targets TD<1%/BD<5%. Gives PSP-level ranges: Razorpay 93-96%, PayU 91-94%, Cashfree 92-95%, direct NPCI integration 95-97%. Volume anchor: 22.35 billion UPI transactions in April 2026. CRITICAL SELF-CAVEAT the parent analysis must carry: 'per-PSP success-rate ranges are not officially published by Razorpay, PayU, or Cashfree. The figures...are aggregated from merchant audits, case studies, and PSP-published optimisation blogs; treat them as directional.' So Claim 2's 92-96% band is industry-blog synthesis, NOT regulator primary data — the TD ~0.7-0.8% half is NPCI-traceable, the merchant-blended half is not. Source type: industry-report (secondary).

results.title: UPI autopay revocations hit 20 mn per month on low customer balance (Business Standard, 7 Sep 2025)
results.snippet: The ORIGIN of Claim 1's '>20 million monthly revocations' figure. 'More than 20 million AutoPay mandates on UPI are revoked each month as users' accounts fall short of the required balances' — revocation follows debit execution failure for insufficient funds, across OTT subscriptions, loan repayments, investments and utilities. FALSIFICATION-RELEVANT FINDING: every 2026 restatement of the 20mn number traces back to this single Sep-2025 Business Standard article; no independent 2026 re-measurement of the revocation count was located, and NPCI does not publish a 'revocations' line item in retrievable form. Treat 20mn/month as a Sep-2025 datapoint being repeated, not as a verified Aug-2026 figure — the volume base has roughly tripled since, so the absolute number is more likely stale-low than stale-high. Source type: press.

results.title: Autopay Ecosystem Statistics — NPCI official product statistics
results.snippet: Primary NPCI AutoPay dataset (mandate creation, active mandates, executions, bank-wise). Returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, but figures surfaced via search index give the growth trajectory needed to date-check Claim 1: July 2025 — 50mn+ new mandates registered (vs 26mn July 2024), 808mn mandate executions (vs 392mn); November 2025 — 1.27 billion recurring mandates processed, top-10 banks 926mn (vs 530.5mn Nov 2024); March 2026 — AutoPay mandates up 35% YoY with 120mn+ recurring transactions monthly (note: this 120mn figure conflicts with the 1.27bn Nov-2025 and 1.6bn May-2026 execution counts, so it is likely a different metric — mandate registrations, not executions — and should NOT be quoted without resolving which base it uses). Source type: regulator (primary, partially retrieved via index).

results.title: Strategic Imperatives from the RBI Payment Systems Report for 2026 and Ahead (NPST)
results.snippet: RBI-side primary framing for the recurring-payments problem. RBI Payment Systems Report (June 2025) puts UPI at ~85.5% of total digital payment transaction volume, and notes NACH Debit — the rail powering EMIs and subscriptions — grew at 27% value CAGR. Useful as the regulator-anchored denominator for any mandate-failure magnitude. HONEST EMPTY CELL: no 2026 RBI report figure was found that breaks out e-mandate failure rate or insufficient-funds share of declines; the only hard auto-debit bounce number surfacing in search is stale NPCI NACH data from March 2021 (32.76% of auto-debit transactions failed by volume — 61.88mn successful of 92.04mn initiated), which is five years old, COVID-era, and NACH not UPI AutoPay, so it must NOT be used as a 2026 proxy. Source type: industry-report on regulator primary.

claims.claim: Indian e-commerce COD orders have an average return-to-origin (RTO) rate of roughly 20-25%, rising to nearly 40% for some brands/categories — a directly checkable benchmark for the RTO magnitude Razorpay measures but does not publish.
claims.quote: average RTO rate of about 20-25%

claims.claim: GoKwik's own network data across 180M+ shoppers puts the national RTO average at 23.18%, with Bihar the worst state at 34.06% annually — i.e. RTO varies by geography by more than 10 percentage points.
claims.quote: Analysis based on "180 Mn+ shoppers"; national average: "23.18%"; Bihar state RTO rate: "34.06% annually"

claims.claim: Cost per RTO on a ₹1,000 COD order is ₹200-250 with zero offsetting revenue, because forward shipping/handling costs ~₹200 and reverse logistics adds ~₹85, versus ~₹100 total cost on a prepaid order — giving a per-incident unit economics figure for the RTO problem.
claims.quote: brands lose ₹200-250 [per RTO while] earning zero revenue ... Additional reverse logistics cost on RTO: INR 85/- ... Prepaid order cost comparison: only about INR 100/-

claims.claim: Most RTO is a demand-side intent problem rather than a logistics problem: 60-70% of RTOs stem from low buying intent versus 20-25% from logistics issues — implying the addressable lever is checkout-time risk scoring, not delivery ops.
claims.quote: 60-70% of RTOs stem from low buying intent ... 20-25% result from logistics issues

claims.claim: Vendor case studies claim large RTO reductions are achievable (Boult 40.21% decrease in COD-led RTO; Lenskart held RTO at 15-19% while COD orders rose 195%), but these are unaudited vendor-marketing numbers with no published baseline or methodology.
claims.quote: Boult: "40.21% decrease in COD-led RTO" ... Lenskart: "195%" increase in COD orders; maintained RTO "between 15-19%"

claims.claim: RBI's Ombudsman Scheme received 13,34,244 complaints in FY2024-25, a 13.55% increase over 11,75,075 in FY2023-24 — establishing a regulator-sourced magnitude for Indian financial-services grievance volume, but at the bank/NBFC level, not the payment-aggregator level.
claims.quote: Total complaints: 13,34,244 in FY25 ... 13.55% rise from 11,75,075 in FY24

claims.claim: Loans & Advances (29.25%) and Credit Cards (20.04%) are the two largest RBI Ombudsman complaint categories in FY25 — meaning refunds/payment failures are NOT the leading grievance category in India's official regulator complaint dataset, which undercuts using this dataset as evidence for the claim that refunds are the single most frequent complaint category against Razorpay.
claims.quote: Loans & Advances: 29.25% (highest); Credit Cards: 20.04% (second highest)

claims.claim: Mobile/Electronic Banking complaints DECREASED 12.74% year-over-year and ATM/Debit Card complaints fell to 7.47% in FY25 from 14.56% in FY23, indicating digital-payment-channel grievances are shrinking as a share of regulated-entity complaints — contrarian evidence against a narrative of worsening digital payment failure.
claims.quote: Mobile/Electronic Banking: Decreased by 12.74% Y-o-Y ... ATMs & Debit Cards: Dropped to 7.47% in FY25 from 14.56% in FY23

claims.claim: The RBI Ombudsman Scheme dataset contains no payment-aggregator or merchant-side complaint category and no reported UPI-specific complaint statistic, so it cannot be used as a proxy for Razorpay merchant refund, settlement or fund-hold complaint rates — a genuine evidence gap for the research question.
claims.quote: The report mentions no specific UPI complaint category statistics.

claims.claim: Complaints are attributed 81.53% to banks and 14.80% to NBFCs, with private sector banks (37.53%) exceeding public sector banks (34.80%) — confirming the dataset's scope is regulated deposit-taking/lending entities, excluding non-bank payment aggregators like Razorpay.
claims.quote: Banks: 81.53% of complaints; NBFCs: 14.80%; Private sector banks: 37.53%; Public sector banks: 34.80%

claims.claim: Global average cart abandonment rate is 70.22% in 2026 (Razorpay Learn citing Baymard Institute), i.e. ~7 of 10 shoppers who add to cart never pay — this is the headline magnitude for the checkout-abandonment domain, though it is a global not India-specific figure.
claims.quote: In 2026, the global average cart abandonment rate is 70.22%.

claims.claim: Mobile checkout abandons at 80.02% versus 66.41% on desktop, and Razorpay states over 60% of Indian e-commerce traffic is mobile — implying the effective Indian blended abandonment rate sits nearer the mobile figure than the global average.
claims.quote: Mobile abandonment rate is 80.02% vs 66.41% on desktop... Since over 60% of Indian e-commerce traffic comes from mobile, this is the single most important benchmark

claims.claim: Razorpay's own benchmark for a well-performing Indian D2C brand is an abandonment rate below 65%, and it asserts Indian D2C brands convert at ~2% versus ~10% for Amazon and Flipkart — a 5x conversion gap Razorpay attributes partly to checkout friction.
claims.quote: Most Indian D2C brands convert at 2%... Amazon and Flipkart convert at 10%

claims.claim: Razorpay publishes NO measured effect of Magic Checkout on abandonment or conversion on this page; it positions the product only qualitatively via prefill across a claimed 100 million+ shopper network, leaving the 'Magic Checkout measured effect' magnitude unfilled by this source.
claims.quote: reducing checkout friction by pre-filling customer details across a network of 100 million+ shoppers

claims.claim: The only quantified upside claim on the page — a 35.26% conversion lift from fixing checkout usability — is sourced to Baymard Institute, not to Razorpay merchant data, so Razorpay offers no first-party checkout-recovery benchmark despite processing the transactions.
claims.quote: Addressing checkout usability issues alone can increase conversion rates by 35.26% (Baymard Institute)

publishDate: 2025-01-29 (stated publish date; content contains 2026-dated benchmarks, so the page has been updated since — last-updated date not disclosed)

claims.claim: In India's D2C festive quarter (FY2026), COD orders returned to origin at a 58% rate versus under 15% for prepaid orders — a ~43-percentage-point RTO gap that quantifies the COD-driven RTO problem Razorpay's RTO Shield agent targets but publishes no benchmark for.
claims.quote: During the festive quarter, COD orders returned at 58%. Prepaid orders? Under 15%.

claims.claim: Blended RTO for Indian D2C brands peaked at 39.2% during the FY2026 festive period, meaning more than one in three orders came back to the seller.

results.snippet: CLAIM 3 CONFIRMED from a Razorpay-authored source — the strongest possible citation for the regulation-vs-practice gap. States the standard cycle is T+2 working days from capture, that only merchants with strong transaction history and low chargeback rates may REQUEST T+1, and that under RBI Payment Aggregator Directions 2025 aggregators must credit merchant funds no later than T+1 banking day, described as 'a contractual right merchants can demand.' results.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025 — RBI Master Direction (primary regulator text)
results.snippet: FALSIFIES the regulatory premise of Claim 3. The Master Direction's Table 1, row 'Credit to merchant's a/c', reads: 'As per the agreement between the PA and the merchant. Such an agreement should be fair, equitable and must transparently mention the settlement timelines.' RBI does NOT prescribe T+1 (or any fixed Ts/T+n period) in the 2025 consolidated Directions — it replaced the earlier prescriptive settlement clocks with a contractual-transparency standard. Therefore Razorpay's T+2 default is NOT a regulation-vs-practice violation; it is permitted, provided it is disclosed in the merchant agreement. Claim 3 as worded ('RBI mandates T+1') should be rewritten as a DISCLOSURE/fairness question, not a compliance gap. Also relevant to Claim 4: para 16(a)/Table 1 sets escrow permitted debits (merchant payouts, refunds, onward settlement to other PAs, PA commission) and states 'Pre-funding: Allowed. Withdrawal of pre-funding: Not permitted' — i.e. RBI constrains what may leave escrow but does NOT define fund-hold triggers or maximum hold durations, leaving fund holds regulator-unspecified and PA-discretionary. Source type: regulator.

results.title: About Settlements — Razorpay Developer Docs (official product documentation)
results.snippet: CONFIRMS the practice half of Claim 3 from Razorpay-official (not marketing) documentation: 'The standard settlement cycle for domestic payments is T+2 working days (where T is the date of transaction capture).' Working days exclude Sundays, 2nd/4th Saturdays and bank holidays — so worst-case real-world settlement stretches well beyond 2 calendar days. Two further lines are unsolved-problem markers per source-type (e): 'The settlement cycle is subject to bank approval and can vary based on your business vertical, risk factors and so on' — i.e. the merchant's own cash-conversion cycle is set unilaterally by a risk assessment the merchant cannot see or query via API; and the docs expose a 'settlements on hold' dashboard state without documenting hold triggers, expected duration, or a resolution path. Razorpay monetises the gap itself via paid Instant Settlements, which is evidence the T+2 delay is a real merchant pain point priced as a product. Source type: Razorpay-official.

results.title: Settlement Transparency: The Complete Merchant Playbook for Questioning Your Payment Gateway in 2026 — Razorpay Blog, 11 June 2026
results.snippet: The single most useful artefact for Claim 3, because Razorpay contradicts itself in public and dated 2026. This post asserts 'Under the RBI Payment Aggregator Directions 2025, aggregators must credit merchant funds no later than T+1 banking day' — which the RBI primary text above does not support — while Razorpay's own docs set the default at T+2. So the 'regulation vs practice gap' is real but is a gap between Razorpay's marketing content and Razorpay's product docs, not between RBI and Razorpay. Also supplies rail-level settlement asymmetry ('UPI typically settles on T+1', 'cards commonly follow T+2 in practice') and links settlement to Claim 4: 'gateways may place holds for volume spikes, high chargeback ratios, or suspected fraud', with the recommended remedy being that merchants 'negotiate clear hold triggers, defined review timelines, and an escalation path' — an admission that these are today negotiated ad hoc rather than systematised. NO MAGNITUDE: the post gives no frequency, percentage, or value of delayed settlements or holds. Source type: Razorpay-marketing.

results.title: What to Do When Your Payment Gateway Account Is Frozen: A 2026 Action Plan — Razorpay Blog, 9 June 2026
results.snippet: CONFIRMS Claim 4 almost verbatim, with dates. Defines the three distinct states the prior analysis conflated: freeze ('stops your account from processing new transactions and pauses settlements'), funds hold ('pauses settlement of specific transactions or a defined amount while the gateway investigates'), and settlement reserve ('a percentage of your settlements held back as a buffer against future chargebacks or refunds'). Trigger list matches Claim 4: chargeback ratios that 'consistently cross 1%, while the global e-commerce average sits near 0.60%'; volume spikes where 'a 10x jump during a festive sale or product launch can look like fraud'; KYC/GST gaps — 'Outdated PAN, GST, address proof, or director details can trigger Payment Aggregator compliance flags'; plus MCC mismatch, restricted categories, and cybercrime/court-order regulatory holds. Resolution bands match exactly: KYC 2–5 business days, chargeback/fraud reviews 1–3 weeks, legal/regulatory holds 30 days or longer. Caveat for the falsification job: the 0.60% and 1% figures are asserted without citation, and no rolling-reserve percentage is published. Source type: Razorpay-marketing (SEO content, not policy).

results.title: Payment Gateway Account Freeze: Resolution Guide India 2026 — Razorpay Blog, 30 April 2026
results.snippet: Second, earlier Razorpay freeze article — useful as a CONSISTENCY TEST that partly undercuts Claim 4's resolution bands. It gives materially different timeframes for overlapping situations: KYC 'resolution typically follows within 24–72 hours after correct document submission', unpaid dues 'auto-unfreeze within 24–48 hours', dormant accounts '1–3 business days'. Two Razorpay posts six weeks apart therefore publish incompatible KYC resolution bands (24–72 hours vs 2–5 business days), which means the bands cited in Claim 4 are content-marketing estimates, not an SLA. Adds trigger detail not in the June post: PMLA provisions, and 'A single third-party payment from a fraud-linked transaction can trigger a full debit freeze' — a genuine merchant-side systemic risk (bank-level lien from someone else's fraud) that no Razorpay agent addresses. Supports Claim 4's core assertion that fund holds are a live, unowned problem. Source type: Razorpay-marketing.

results.title: RBI issues consolidated Reserve Bank of India (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025 — AZB & Partners (independent legal analysis)
results.snippet: Independent legal confirmation of the RBI reading, so Claim 3's falsification does not rest on a single fetch. AZB and parallel commentary (Lexology, IndiaCorpLaw, Khaitan) describe the 2025 consolidation as 'liberalising' settlement: 'settlement credits to merchants can now be effected in accordance with the agreement between the PA and the merchant, provided such agreements are fair, equitable, and transparently disclose the settlement timelines.' Also confirms the escrow regime (segregation of merchant funds from PA funds in a designated commercial bank; existing non-bank PAs to migrate within two months of authorisation) and the merchant-agreement transparency duty covering MDR, set-up and maintenance fees. Net effect on the analysis: the compliance angle for Claim 3 is dead, but a WEAKER and still-defensible problem survives — merchants have no standardised, machine-readable view of their contracted settlement timeline, hold triggers or reserve terms, and RBI now places the burden of that transparency squarely on the PA. Source type: industry-report / legal commentary.

claims.claim: Razorpay's standard settlement is T+2 working days as of Aug 2026, corroborating the regulation-vs-practice gap against RBI Payment Aggregator Directions' T+1 expectation (independent third-party confirmation, not Razorpay's own docs).
claims.quote: Standard settlement is T+2 working days, meaning funds reach your bank two working days after the customer pays.

claims.claim: Sudden account limitations, fund withholding during compliance reviews, and rolling reserves are Razorpay's single most serious merchant complaint, triggered by atypical volume spikes or documentation gaps — matching the trigger list in the prior analysis (volume spikes, KYC/GST gaps, PA compliance flags).
claims.quote: The most serious complaint is sudden account limitations and fund withholding during compliance reviews, triggered by atypical volume spikes or documentation gaps.

claims.claim: CONTRARIAN to the claim that refunds are the most frequent complaint category: this review's aggregated complaint taxonomy names payment holds, disputes and unresponsive support — and contains no mention of refunds at all. Trustpilot stands at 1.4/5 across 437 reviews with those three themes; G2 4.3/5 (150 reviews), Capterra 3.6/5 (114 reviews).
claims.quote: Trustpilot (razorpay.com) 1.4/5 (437 reviews) Payment holds, disputes, unresponsive support

claims.claim: Slow, template-driven merchant support with long resolution times is the single most common criticism of Razorpay across review sites, specifically when a dispute, freeze, or onboarding issue arises — evidencing an OPEN operations/support-automation problem.
claims.quote: Small and mid-sized businesses repeatedly report long resolution times and canned responses when a payment dispute, freeze, or onboarding issue arises.

claims.claim: A merchant-reported blended payment success rate of 93%+ on Razorpay is consistent with the 92-96% merchant-observed band, supporting the finding that residual failure is business decline rather than infrastructure. (Single anecdotal G2 reviewer, not a measured benchmark.)
claims.quote: one merchant wrote that a '93%+ success rate for me means more money reaching bank account every month,'

claims.claim: Indian SMEs take an average of 73 days to settle invoices (effective DSO), against government norms encouraging 45-day MSME payment — a ~28-day gap, per Recordent's Indian SME Receivables Report 2026 (released 27 June 2026).
claims.quote: Indian SMEs require an average of 73 days to settle invoices, highlighting the necessity for stronger receivables management and improved payment discipline.

claims.claim: The average Indian SME in the sample carries approximately Rs 3.83 crore in receivables unpaid beyond 360 days — i.e. locked-up working capital sitting past a full year.
claims.quote: The report indicates that the average SME carries approximately ₹3.83 crore in receivables unpaid beyond 360 days, demonstrating substantial locked-up capital affecting business liquidity and financial stability.

claims.claim: 82.6% of Indian SME invoices are issued with credit terms of 0-30 days, so the ~73-day realised payment cycle represents a collection-discipline failure of roughly 43+ days beyond contracted terms, not lax credit policy.
claims.quote: Despite government regulations encouraging MSME payment within 45 days, 82.6% of invoices are issued with credit terms of 0–30 days. This indicates the challenge stems from payment discipline rather than credit policy.

claims.claim: Payment cycles vary materially by geography — Mumbai settles invoices fastest among metros at 59 days versus the 73-day national average — indicating receivables stress is unevenly distributed rather than uniform.
claims.quote: Mumbai leads metro cities at 59 days for invoice settlement

claims.claim: The underlying dataset is vendor-generated: ~1.1 lakh MSMEs and 10+ lakh transaction-level data points drawn from Recordent, a commercial credit-risk and collections platform whose CEO uses the findings to advocate purchasing 'receivables intelligence solutions' — so the magnitudes are self-selected toward businesses already experiencing collection problems and are not an independently audited national benchmark.
claims.quote: Winny Patro, Founder and CEO of Recordent, stated: "Greater transparency, stronger credit governance and wider adoption of receivables intelligence solutions can be a game changer."

claims.claim: As of June 2026 (reporting on May 2026 data), only ~30% of UPI AutoPay auto-debit transactions at SBI — the largest remitter bank — are successfully approved, with ~70% failing. This confirms the Sep-2025 SBI figure is still being reported a year later, so falsification attempt on Finding 1's SBI leg FAILS.
claims.quote: For SBI, the ecosystem's largest remitter bank, only about 30% of auto-debit transactions are successfully approved.

claims.claim: The dominant cause of UPI AutoPay mandate failure is business decline (insufficient funds at the moment the mandate triggers), not technical/infrastructure decline — corroborating Finding 2's business-vs-technical split for the mandate/subscription domain specifically.
claims.quote: The remaining 70% fail, predominantly due to business-related issues such as insufficient funds at the moment the mandate is triggered.

claims.claim: UPI e-mandate volume at the top ten remitter banks reached ~1.6 billion transactions in May 2026, up ~3x from 577 million in May 2025 — supplying the missing denominator for mandate-failure magnitude (at a ~70% SBI-style failure rate this implies hundreds of millions of failed auto-debits per month, i.e. the involuntary-churn / subscription-recovery problem is growing ~3x YoY).
claims.quote: In May, the top ten remitter banks cumulatively processed approximately 1.6 billion e-mandate transactions. This represents an almost threefold increase compared to the 577 million transactions processed during the same period just one year prior.

claims.claim: As of June 2026 there is no unified view of a user's active UPI AutoPay mandates across apps; NPCI is only now building a centralized API so third-party UPI apps can display them — evidence that mandate visibility/management is an unsolved, infrastructure-level operational gap (and that mandate cancellation still bounces users back to the originating app).
claims.quote: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) is developing a centralized application programming interface (API) that will allow all third-party UPI applications (TPAPs) to display a user's entire list of active electronic mandates in one unified dashboard.

claims.claim: This article does NOT contain the '>20 million UPI AutoPay mandates revoked monthly for insufficient balance' figure, so that specific leg of Finding 1 remains unconfirmed by this 2026 source and still needs direct NPCI monthly AutoPay data to verify.
claims.quote: The article does not contain a specific figure regarding "20 million/crore mandate revocation"

claims.claim: The largest single category of merchant-side UPI failures is bank server timeout at 35-45% of failures — larger than insufficient balance (15-25%) — which cuts against the Phase 1 finding that residual UPI failure is 'mostly BUSINESS decline, not infrastructure'. Combining the page's own buckets, technical/infrastructure causes (bank timeout 35-45% + network 10-15%) total roughly 45-60% of failures versus roughly 35-55% for business causes (wrong PIN 20-30% + insufficient balance 15-25%).
claims.quote: Failure category breakdown (merchant-side): 'Bank server timeout | 35-45% | Partially [actionable]'; 'Wrong UPI PIN / exceeded attempts | 20-30% | Yes'; 'Insufficient balance | 15-25% | Yes'; 'Network/connectivity issues | 10-15% | Partially'; 'Account blocked/deactivated | 5-10% | No'

claims.claim: Merchant-observed blended UPI success rates in India are 92-96% as of 2026, corroborating the existing Phase 1 figure — but the source explicitly disclaims these as unverified estimates rather than published benchmarks.
claims.quote: 'Typical merchant-side blended success rate | 92-96%' — with the note that PSP-level numbers are 'directional, not benchmark numbers' and 'not officially published.'

claims.claim: System-wide UPI technical decline (TD) is ~0.7-0.8% as of 2025, down from 8-10% in 2016, against NPCI circular OC-149 (June 2022) targets of TD <1% and BD <5%, implying a regulatory-target blended success rate above ~94%.
claims.quote: 'System-wide TD in 2025 | ~0.7-0.8%'; 'System-wide TD in 2016 | 8-10%'; 'NPCI Technical Decline (TD) target | <1% | Circular OC-149 (June 2022)'; 'NPCI Business Decline (BD) target | <5%'; 'Combined, those targets imply a blended success rate above ~94%'

claims.claim: No officially published, audited per-PSP UPI success-rate benchmark exists for Razorpay; the only available figures (Razorpay 93-96%, PayU 91-94%, Cashfree 92-95%, direct NPCI 95-97%) are self-described as unofficial and directional — supporting the Phase 1 verdict that Razorpay's performance numbers lack an independent baseline.
claims.quote: 'Razorpay | 93-96%' ... Note: these are 'directional, not benchmark numbers' and 'not officially published.'

claims.claim: Smart retry logic recovers 20-30% of UPI timeout failures and in-app UPI SDKs improve success rates by 2-4 percentage points — a quantified but unaudited magnitude for the failed-payment-recovery problem domain.
claims.quote: 'Smart retry logic recovers 20-30% of timeout failures'; 'In-app UPI SDKs improve success rates by 2-4%'

claims.claim: Razorpay itself puts a number on Indian finance-team reconciliation effort: 20-40 work hours per month spent on reconciliation when a merchant uses multiple payment gateways. This is the only Razorpay-published magnitude found for the 'reconciliation effort' gap in JOB 2, but it is an unaudited vendor-marketing figure with no stated methodology, sample size, or baseline.
claims.quote: save your finance teams 20-40 work hours a month in doing reconciliations

claims.claim: Multi-gateway settlement reconciliation at Razorpay merchants is an explicitly MANUAL process: finance teams must download files from each payment aggregator and reconcile payments against settlements by hand to confirm they are in sync — confirming reconciliation as an open, labour-borne problem rather than an automated one.
claims.quote: Finance teams have to download and manually reconcile payments and settlements from various payment aggregators to make sure the payments and settlement are in sync.

claims.claim: Late authorization creates a reconciliation exception class that Razorpay does not resolve automatically: payment status can be finalised minutes to several hours after the transaction, forcing finance staff to repeatedly re-check pending transactions before books will balance. This is a concrete, Razorpay-authored description of unresolved exception handling.
claims.quote: For some payments, the actual status of the payment is generated later, and the delay in the status of the payment update can extend from a few minutes to several hours.

claims.claim: Razorpay acknowledges merchants lack visibility into the settlement cycle and payment flow, and that manual reconciliation effort spikes at month-end — a stated FINANCE-domain problem in Razorpay's own words, with settlement delays ranging from a few hours to a few days.
claims.quote: Lack of visibility on the settlement cycle and payments flow for the business; An increase in manual effort to complete reconciliation at month-end

claims.claim: Razorpay's named product response to reconciliation is Optimizer's Single View Recon — a consolidated VIEWING dashboard (transaction status, UTR numbers, Settlement IDs, processing aggregator) shipped June 2022, not an automated exception-resolution or auto-matching engine. It surfaces mismatches for humans rather than resolving them, so the reconciliation-exception gap remains open four years later and is not covered by any of the 7 Agent Studio prebuilt agents.
claims.quote: all payments and settlement information for your business...in one dashboard

claims.claim: Razorpay's Agent Studio launch blog names refunds explicitly as part of the merchant pain surface it targets, yet the agent line-up shipped contains no refund agent — confirming refunds are an acknowledged-but-uncovered problem (supports claim 5 and claim 8's gap list).
claims.quote: Financial performance depends on everything that happens around the transaction, including dispute management, reconciliation, failed payment recovery, refunds, payouts, and many more.

claims.claim: The Agent Studio launch page lists eight agent cards covering seven distinct functions — Dispute Responder, Subscription Recovery, Abandoned Cart Conversion (shipped in two partner-powered variants, SuperU and Nugget by Zomato), Cashflow Forecaster, RTO Shield, RTO Insights, and Settlement Insights — matching the prior finding's seven agents but revealing that Abandoned Cart is delivered by third parties, not Razorpay itself.
claims.quote: Abandoned Cart Conversion (Powered by SuperU) ... Abandoned Cart Conversion (Powered by Nugget by Zomato)

claims.claim: The page contains no mention whatsoever of fund holds, account freezes, refund failures, B2B receivables/collections, GST/TDS line matching, or reconciliation exception resolution — none of these has a shipped agent, so the prior finding's coverage-gap list survives falsification.
claims.quote: Third-party builders will be able to create and publish specialized agents

claims.claim: As of the 12 Mar 2026 launch, only the No-Code Agent Builder is explicitly labelled beta while the core agents are described as launching, and access is gated behind an invitation/early-access request rather than general availability — a partial refinement of the claim that 'Agent Studio remains in early access/beta'.
claims.quote: we are introducing a No-Code Agent Builder (beta) that will enable operations and finance teams to create custom agents tailored to their business logic

claims.claim: Razorpay's own Agent Studio announcement publishes zero performance metrics — no dispute win-rate lift, no recovery rate, no RTO reduction percentage, no baseline or methodology — so there is no company-authored magnitude for any of the problems the agents claim to solve.
claims.quote: Detects high-risk COD orders before dispatch using LLM address validation and bad pincode intelligence.

claims.claim: Razorpay's own blog states card transactions are typically settled T+2 working days while UPI settles T+1 — confirming a live gap between practice and the RBI Payment Aggregator Directions 2025 T+1 mandate that the same article cites. This corroborates rather than falsifies established finding #3, though it refines it: the T+2 default applies to cards, not to all methods (UPI is already T+1).
claims.quote: Card transactions are typically settled on T+2 working days, while UPI transactions are generally settled on T+1.

claims.claim: Razorpay-official content confirms RBI Payment Aggregator Directions 2025 impose a hard T+1 credit obligation on aggregators, i.e. the regulatory ceiling is T+1 banking day, with the article elsewhere noting penalties under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 reaching Rs 1 crore for certain violations.
claims.quote: Under the RBI Payment Aggregator Directions 2025, aggregators must credit merchant funds no later than T+1 banking day.

claims.claim: Merchant fund holds remain an unsolved, contract-negotiated problem as of June 2026: Razorpay's own advice is that merchants must negotiate hold triggers, review timelines and an escalation path into their gateway contract — there is no automated product or agent that resolves holds, and 'unilateral, indefinite holds with no reporting' are named as a live red flag. Named triggers are volume spikes, high chargeback ratios, and suspected fraud. No magnitude (frequency, duration, value held) is published.
claims.quote: Gateways may place holds for volume spikes, high chargeback ratios, or suspected fraud. Negotiate clear hold triggers, defined review timelines, and an escalation path into your contract.

claims.claim: Settlement reconciliation is manual and breaks when reports lack transaction-level linkage: Razorpay lists the fields a settlement report must itemise (MDR, GST on MDR, refund offsets, chargeback deductions, net settled amount, bank UTR) and flags 'net-only reporting' and missing UTRs as failure modes that make payouts impossible to match to bank credits — evidence that reconciliation exception handling is an open merchant problem. No hours/FTE magnitude is given.
claims.quote: Net-only reporting with no transaction linkage. Missing UTRs, so payouts cannot be matched to bank credits.

claims.claim: The article's only quantified merchant-risk figure is a global, non-India, three-year-stale chargeback cost estimate — indicating Razorpay publishes no India-specific chargeback or merchant-fraud rate benchmark, leaving that magnitude gap unfilled.
claims.quote: Global chargebacks cost merchants an estimated $100 billion in 2023

claims.claim: India's MSME Samadhaan portal had accumulated 2,56,892 delayed-payment applications from micro and small enterprises worth Rs 55,244 crore, with Rs 20,979 crore of claims still pending, as of 14 August 2026 — a citable floor-magnitude for the B2B receivables/collections problem that no Razorpay agent addresses.
claims.quote: As of August 14, 2026, MSME Samadhaan data showed that micro and small enterprises had filed 256,892 applications involving delayed payments worth Rs 55,244 crore, with claims amounting to Rs 20,979 crore still pending.

claims.claim: 40,580 delayed-payment applications — 16% of all filings on MSME Samadhaan — had remained unresolved for more than a year, i.e. receivables disputes routinely exceed 365 days to resolve, far beyond any DSO norm.
claims.quote: Around 40,580 applications, or 16%, had remained unresolved for more than a year, pointing to substantial working capital being locked in delayed or disputed receivables.

claims.claim: Delayed payment to MSMEs was severe enough in Aug 2026 that Parliament legislated new time-bound machinery (mediation within 90 days of first appearance, arbitration referral within 30 days, award within 90 days of pleadings) — implying the pre-existing statutory 45-day payment rule and MSEFC process were not working.
claims.quote: Mediation would have to conclude within 90 days from the date fixed for first appearance, while disputes that fail mediation would be referred to arbitration within 30 days, with awards required within 90 days of completion of pleadings.

claims.claim: Crisil Intelligence characterises Indian MSME delayed payments as a credit-discipline failure on the scale that the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was created to fix, and explicitly frames the remedy as conditional on implementation — i.e. as of Aug 2026 the problem is OPEN, not solved.
claims.quote: By introducing time-bound dispute resolution for individual stages, strengthening the enforceability of awards and enhancing the role of facilitation councils, the Bill can improve payment discipline and unlock working capital across the MSME sector.

claims.claim: CAVEAT ON THIS SOURCE'S NUMBERS: the identical cumulative totals (2,56,892 applications / Rs 55,244 crore) are elsewhere reported as the Samadhaan position as of 31 December 2025, so the ANI/India Gazette '14 August 2026' as-of date is likely a restatement of a stale portal snapshot and the figures should be treated as cumulative-since-inception, not a 2026 flow.
claims.quote: 2,56,892 delayed-payment applications involving ₹55,244.31 crore

claims.claim: Razorpay's own official developer documentation states the standard domestic settlement cycle is T+2 working days from transaction capture — directly corroborating the claimed regulation-vs-practice gap against RBI Payment Aggregator Directions' T+1 requirement (this is the company's own current-state documentation, not a third-party allegation, so it cannot be dismissed as outdated reporting).
claims.quote: The standard settlement cycle for domestic payments is **T+2** working days (where **T** is the date of transaction capture).

claims.claim: Faster-than-T+2 settlement is NOT the default and is not self-serve: Razorpay's Instant Settlements is an on-demand feature that requires the merchant to raise a manual support ticket to activate, meaning the default merchant experience remains T+2 unless they discover and request an add-on product.
claims.quote: This is an on-demand feature. Please raise a request with our [Support team](https://razorpay.com/support/#request) to get this feature activated on your Razorpay account.

claims.claim: Settlement failure is a documented, recurring operational condition in Razorpay's system, with enumerated causes including frozen/inactive merchant bank accounts, incorrect bank details, and bank-side rejection — establishing settlement-failure exception handling as a real merchant problem, though the docs attach no frequency or magnitude to it.
claims.quote: Some reasons for settlement failure: Your bank account is inactive or frozen. Incorrect bank account details. The settlement was rejected by your bank.

claims.claim: Razorpay ships a 'settlements placed on hold' capability in the Dashboard, confirming that settlement holds are a first-class, productised state in the platform — but this settlements documentation page exposes no triggers, no resolution timeline, and no automated remediation path for a merchant whose funds are held, consistent with the claim that fund holds are an uncovered problem.
claims.quote: Enable settlements on hold

claims.claim: Razorpay does not publish a fixed settlement cycle for international payments, deferring instead to unspecified applicable law and requiring merchants to check their own Dashboard — so no public benchmark exists for cross-border settlement timing.
claims.quote: The default settlement cycle for international payments is as per applicable law(s).

publishDate: No publication or last-updated date is exposed on the page; content retrieved and verified 2026-08-24. As live product documentation it should be treated as describing the current (Aug 2026) state.

claims.claim: The RBI (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025 do NOT mandate a T+1 settlement cycle; they delegate settlement day-counts to the PA–merchant contract, requiring only that the timeline be disclosed transparently. This directly falsifies the Phase-1 claim that Razorpay's T+2 standard settlement violates an RBI T+1 mandate — there is no regulation-vs-practice gap on settlement timing in this Master Direction.
claims.quote: Credit to merchant's a/c: As per the agreement between the PA and the merchant. Such an agreement should be fair, equitable and must transparently mention the settlement timelines.

claims.claim: The Master Direction is RBI/DPSS/2025-26/141, dated September 15, 2025, effective immediately, and applies to all bank and non-bank PAs — so it is the operative regulator text as of Aug 2026 and supersedes reliance on the older 2020 PA/PG guidelines that did carry Ts+1/Tp+1 day-count timelines.
claims.quote: These Directions shall be effective immediately unless indicated otherwise for any specific provision herein.

claims.claim: Merchant due-diligence/KYC is a hard regulatory obligation with a dated cliff: merchants onboarded up to December 31, 2025 must be brought into compliance within one year, and from January 1, 2026 due diligence must happen at onboarding, with the PA retrieving the merchant's KYC record from CKYCR. This gives a regulator-grounded basis for the 'KYC/GST gaps' fund-hold trigger in claim 4 — PAs are legally compelled to freeze or block non-compliant merchants rather than doing so discretionarily.
claims.quote: From January 1, 2026, merchants should be onboarded in accordance with due diligence requirements.

claims.claim: PAs are prohibited from routing Cash-on-Delivery transactions through the escrow account, meaning COD flows (the segment where RTO/return-to-origin loss occurs) sit entirely outside the regulated PA settlement rail — so no PA-side settlement or escrow protection applies to COD, and RTO cost falls on the merchant.
claims.quote: The escrow account shall not be operated for 'Cash-on-Delivery' transactions.

claims.claim: Customer chargeback rights are explicitly preserved by regulation, and refunds/reversals must route through the escrow account, which means a PA cannot contractually limit chargeback exposure or settle refunds outside escrow — placing the reconciliation and funding burden for disputes structurally on the PA and merchant.
claims.quote: The chargeback rights of customers, as applicable, shall remain unaffected.

claims.claim: More than 20 million UPI AutoPay mandates are revoked every month in India because the user's bank account lacks sufficient balance at debit execution — confirming, not falsifying, the first half of Phase 1 finding #1. NOTE: the assigned URL returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; this text was recovered via search-index extraction of the Business Standard article, so treat the wording as near-verbatim rather than confirmed verbatim.
claims.quote: More than 20 million AutoPay mandates on the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) are revoked each month as users' accounts fall short of the required balances. ... The revocations stand at 20 million every month due to debit execution failure because there is not enough money in the user's bank account where the mandate was created. (Business Standard, https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/upi-autopay-revocations-hit-20-mn-monthly-over-low-customer-balances-125090700500_1.html, 7 Sep 2025, source type: press reporting NPCI data)

claims.claim: The SBI ~30% auto-debit approval rate (~70% failure) is STILL being reported as current in mid-2026, not just Sep 2025 — the freshness challenge in Phase 1 finding #1 does not refute it. Failure is attributed predominantly to insufficient funds, i.e. BUSINESS decline, which independently corroborates Phase 1 finding #2.
claims.quote: State Bank of India (SBI): 'only about 30% of auto-debit transactions are successfully approved' ... Remaining 70% fail predominantly due to insufficient funds. (The420.in, https://the420.in/npci-unified-e-mandate-tracking-upi-autopay-apps/, 23 June 2026, source type: press)

claims.claim: UPI e-mandate execution volume roughly tripled year-on-year: the top ten remitter banks processed ~1.6 billion e-mandate transactions in May 2026 versus 577 million in May 2025 — meaning the absolute number of failed auto-debits is growing fast even if the failure RATE were flat, which sizes the subscription involuntary-churn problem upward for 2026.
claims.quote: May 2026: Top ten remitter banks processed approximately 1.6 billion e-mandate transactions; May 2025: 577 million transactions (representing a threefold increase year-over-year). (The420.in, https://the420.in/npci-unified-e-mandate-tracking-upi-autopay-apps/, 23 June 2026, source type: press citing NPCI)

claims.claim: New AutoPay mandate registrations nearly doubled year-on-year — over 50 million new mandates registered by remitter banks in July 2025 versus 26 million in July 2024 — providing the denominator context that ~20mn monthly revocations must be read against.
claims.quote: NPCI figures showing that in July 2025, remitter banks registered over 50 million new AutoPay mandates—nearly double the 26 million logged in July 2024. (Business Standard, https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/upi-autopay-revocations-hit-20-mn-monthly-over-low-customer-balances-125090700500_1.html, 7 Sep 2025, source type: press citing NPCI)

claims.claim: The revoked mandates are concentrated in exactly the recurring-revenue categories a payment aggregator monetises — OTT/entertainment subscriptions, loan repayments, investments (SIPs) and utilities — so mandate failure maps directly onto merchant involuntary churn rather than being a consumer-only inconvenience.
claims.quote: Cancellations occurred on recurring payments use cases such as entertainment or over-the-top (OTT) subscriptions, loan repayments, investments and utilities, among other automated payment scenarios. (Business Standard, https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/upi-autopay-revocations-hit-20-mn-monthly-over-low-customer-balances-125090700500_1.html, 7 Sep 2025, source type: press)

claims.claim: Voxya's entire Razorpay complaint corpus is only 34 complaints with 18 resolved (52.94% consumer satisfaction), which is far too small a sample to support any claim about which category is 'the single most frequent complaint against Razorpay' — it FALSIFIES the use of Voxya as a magnitude source for Job 1 claim 5.
claims.quote: The Consumer satisfaction score of Razorpay is 52.94% because out of 34 consumer complaints, only 18 are resolved.

claims.claim: The Voxya Razorpay listing contains NO complaints dated 2026 — the most recent entry is 30 June 2025 — so this source cannot substantiate any 'as of Aug 2026' claim about Razorpay refund complaints being the top category.
claims.quote: SARVESH SANTOSH PADHYE on Jun 30, 2025 Razorpay – Razorpay payment Settlement issue Closed

claims.claim: Refund-related titles are the largest single category in the Voxya Razorpay list (roughly 14 of 34 complaint titles explicitly name a refund not given/failed/not issued), directionally supporting claim 5 that refunds are the most frequent complaint category, but the entries are overwhelmingly END-CONSUMER refunds against Razorpay's merchants, not merchant-side refund API failures.
claims.quote: Pooja Kumari on Aug 24, 2022 Razorpay – Refund failed Open I got a mail from razorpay that my refund is successful, but my bank checked through the RRN number they provided and told

claims.claim: Merchant settlement delay and settlement-on-hold is the dominant category among the MOST RECENT complaints (page 1, 2024-2025), with at least five titles naming unsettled funds — independent corroboration that fund holds/settlement freezes (claim 4) are a live, unresolved merchant problem and that they postdate the refund complaints.
claims.quote: Razorpay – Put the settlement on hold by razorpay ... Razorpay – Payment not settled from 2 months ... Razorpay – Amount not being settled ... Razorpay – Settlement not cleared

claims.claim: Merchant account suspension and chargeback-handling operational failures appear as distinct complaint types with no Razorpay self-service remedy, e.g. an account suspension complaint from a software company and an unresolved ('Open') complaint that Razorpay failed to submit a chargeback representment letter to the bank after the merchant's systems were hacked.
claims.quote: onkar nath on Jun 20, 2022 Razorpay – Razorpay illegally suspending accouts Closed Hi, we are Shavi Soft Solutions, A new delhi based software company. Razor pay has suspended our me... | KMUNOTAG PVT LTD on Mar 10, 2022 Razorpay – Chargeback Letter Not submitted to Bank Open Our systems had been hacked and few users took the money from our Razorpay API accounts.

publishDate: No publish date; live aggregator page, accessed 2026-08-24. Latest complaint on the page is dated 2025-06-30; oldest 2019-01-07.

claims.claim: Razorpay's Vulcan performance figures are explicitly beta results for which Razorpay has published no methodology, no baseline and no sample period — directly confirming (not falsifying) the finding that the Vulcan numbers are unaudited vendor marketing.
claims.quote: The article notes these are "beta results" and that "Razorpay has not published the methodology, baseline or sample period behind them."

claims.claim: The specific Vulcan claims are an 8-10% improvement in payment success rates, 8x more international card fraud detected, and 5x more fraudulent or disputed transactions identified — attributed to Razorpay itself, not to any independent audit or third-party case study.
claims.quote: Razorpay reports: "8-10% improvement in payment success rates" / "8x more international card fraud detected" / "5x more fraudulent or disputed transactions identified"

claims.claim: Vulcan was trained on approximately 4 billion payments and 3 trillion data points, using roughly 3,000 signals per transaction, with architecture and training data proprietary to Razorpay and infrastructure hosted in India — the only concrete, quantified disclosure Razorpay has made about the model.
claims.quote: The model was developed using "4 billion payments. 3 trillion data points. One model trained on all of it," utilizing approximately 3,000 signals per transaction.

claims.claim: Razorpay has not disclosed the legal basis under India's DPDP Act for training its own proprietary model on merchant transaction data for which it acts only as a data processor, has not said whether merchants can opt out of training, and left six MediaNama questions unanswered — an open, unaddressed compliance/risk problem with no Razorpay product or agent covering it.
claims.quote: Under the DPDP Act, data processors may only use information "on the fiduciary's instructions and for the fiduciary's purposes." Training an independent model represents a separate purpose requiring "consent must be free, specific and informed." ... Six questions MediaNama submitted to Razorpay remain unanswered.

claims.claim: Razorpay intends to extend Vulcan beyond payments into authentication and lending, which the reporting flags as raising unresolved fairness and explainability questions for creditworthiness scoring.

claims.claim: As of 12 March 2026, Razorpay's IPO was still 'a few quarters away' with no timeline offered — dated evidence that no public DRHP/RHP existed at that point, consistent with (and predating) the alleged ~12 June 2026 confidential SEBI pre-filing. 1. NO SUCH PROVISION EXISTS. Direct text search of the MD on rbi.org.in for suspend / terminate / block / freeze / withhold / hold / discontinue / exit / cease returns nothing applicable: the MD imposes a due-diligence OBLIGATION on the PA but prescribes NO enforcement mechanism against merchants — no suspension, no termination, no fund hold. The 2025 MD verbatim: "Credit to merchant's a/c: As per the agreement between the PA and the merchant. Such an agreement should be fair, equitable and must transparently mention the settlement timelines." The MD replaced the old T+1/Td+1 prescription with commercially negotiated terms (confirmed by multiple firm summaries via search, Sep-Oct 2025). Settlement withholding is therefore a CONTRACTUAL, PA-discretionary act governed by the merchant agreement — the exact opposite of "legally compelled." Escrow Table 1 permitted debits cover payments to merchants and refunds; no withholding mechanism is authorised.
3. CATEGORY ERROR. "Must complete CDD" ≠ "must freeze funds." The MD's remedy path runs against the PA (authorisation risk), not as a mandated merchant-freeze. A PA choosing to hold funds pending KYC is exercising commercial discretion under its own agreement, which is precisely the discretionary behaviour the claim denies.
4. "GST gaps" — one of the four triggers the claim purports to ground — appears nowhere in the MD. GST/tax reconciliation is not a PA due-diligence item under this Direction, so the claim over-covers claim 4's trigger list.

SECONDARY OVERSTATEMENTS: (a) "within one year" is one year from the MD's date (15 Sep 2025 → 15 Sep 2026), NOT one year from 31 Dec 2025 — the claim leaves the anchor ambiguous and a reader would likely date it to Dec 2026. (b) CKYCR retrieval is conditional ("with the merchant's consent"), and the MD expressly permits alternate CDD where the record is absent from CKYCR or the PA cannot access it (application pending) — the claim states it unconditionally. It may conflate mandate creation, execution, modification and revocation — so a 3x rise in "e-mandate transactions" does not establish a 3x rise in auto-debit EXECUTIONS, which is what the failed-auto-debit inference requires. Separately, the article's own named use cases are "systematic investment plans (SIPs), insurance premiums, media/streaming subscriptions" — SIPs and insurance premiums dominate Indian e-mandate volume and are NOT subscription-commerce churn, so aggregate e-mandate growth does not size Razorpay's merchant-subscription involuntary-churn problem. The claim further concedes it assumes "even if the failure RATE were flat" — an assumption with no supporting evidence in any source found.

NOTE FOR THE PARENT ANALYSIS: the underlying directional idea (UPI AutoPay volume growing fast) may well be true, but it is NOT established at the stated magnitude, for the stated period, by the stated sources. Do not carry the 1.6bn/577mn figures or the "May 2026" dating into the Phase 1 output without a primary NPCI source. If retained at all, it must be labelled: single-source, press-citing-unnamed-NPCI-data, year unstated in source, uncorroborated.

evidence:
ATTEMPTED REFUTATION FAILED — claim survives on four independent legs.

1) SOURCE VERIFIED VERBATIM. medianama.com direct fetch returns HTTP 403 (bot block, not 404), so I retrieved it through a text-extraction proxy (r.jina.ai). (URL as cited: https://www.medianama.com/2026/08/223-razorpay-vulcan-ai-foundation-model-payments/). It contains the exact sentence: "These are Razorpay's own beta results. It has not published the methodology, baseline or sample period behind them." — alongside the figures "8-10% improvement in payment success rates", "8x more international card fraud detected", "5x more fraudulent or disputed transactions identified". 2) PRIMARY-SOURCE CORROBORATION (this is the strongest leg — I went to Razorpay itself, not the secondary source). Razorpay's own launch blog https://razorpay.com/blog/one-foundation-model-built-for-indias-payments-ecosystem/ contains ZERO quantified performance metrics — only qualitative capability descriptions ("Hyper-Precision Routing", "Network-Level Fraud Protection", "The model scores every possible route in real-time...") — and discloses no A/B test, control group, baseline, or sample period. Razorpay's product page https://razorpay.com/foundation-model/ carries the numbers ("8-10% improvement in success rates", "8X more international card fraud detected", "5X more disputed transactions identified") with no methodology, no baseline, no control group, no sample period, no pilot merchant name, and no independent audit. 3) INDEPENDENT THIRD-PARTY CORROBORATION. DataQuest/DQIndia (4 days ago): "Razorpay says Vulcan detects 8x more international card fraud, but enterprises still lack the baseline, audit details and..." — a second outlet reaching the same conclusion independently of MediaNama.

4) SEARCHED FOR CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE — NONE FOUND. Bing queries for a Razorpay Vulcan technical report / whitepaper / benchmark / independent audit returned nothing; no engineering-blog post, no third-party audit, no named customer case study with numbers surfaced. CURRENCY: Vulcan launched 18 Aug 2026 (confirmed via CNBC-TV18, Fortune India, Business Standard, AWS press release, Deccan Herald coverage all dated ~18 Aug 2026). The claim is six days old — not outdated.

So "explicitly beta results" is slightly overstated as to who said it; the substance is nonetheless corroborated by press framing elsewhere (Analytics Insight, 5 days ago: "Early Vulcan deployments show an 8...").
